Pour écrire cet article, je me suis plon: To write this article, I immersed myself in the world of Manioky Café, a place where every dish and every drink carries a memory. There, I sipped a Cola Couronne for the first time and discovered Prestige beer. These flavours opened my eyes to a culinary heritage I knew very little about. What I took away: food is not just a matter of taste, it is a vehicle for identity, memory and culture. Beyond the flavours, what stayed with me were the challenges and the effort it takes to keep these traditions alive thousands of kilometres from the country where they come from.
Écrire cet article a aussi été un défi j: Writing this article was also a journalistic challenge: how do you convey the soul of a place and its cooking through words? Some things can’t be fully translated. But in the end, what I take away is that Manioky Café is much more than a restaurant: it is a space for passing things on, for exchange and for celebration. There, I discovered nearly forgotten dishes, techniques handed down from generation to generation and, above all, the essential role of food in preserving the history of a country and of an entire community.
<strong>Au Manioky Café, chaque plat rac: At Manioky Café, every dish tells the story of Haiti: from sandwiches named after historical figures, like Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, to bites inspired by family recipes. Haitian drinks complete the experience: Cola Couronne, Prestige beer or Barbancourt rum take taste buds on a journey to the heart of the Pearl of the Antilles, without leaving Repentigny. Every bite also tells a family story and the long-held dream of co-owner Cynthia Élie. Meet her.
Mardi 26 août, 10 h. Habituellement, à c: Tuesday, August 26, 10 a.m. At this hour, the kitchen is usually humming with preparations, but on this day, instead of handling pots and pans, Cynthia sits down to share her story. Seated on one of the chairs near the glass door, she lets the memories come back: from a very young age, she was already baking with her grandmother and her mother. That sweet tooth has travelled all the way onto Manioky Café’s menu, where you’ll find emblematic desserts like the moist, fragrant rum cake or the rich, melt-in-your-mouth Tres Leches cake. But far beyond recipes, what these ancestors left her are gestures, a memory and an identity. “They’re no longer with us today,” Cynthia confides sadly, fondly recalling the two women. She especially remembers the rice pudding flavoured with anise and cinnamon that they used to make. “I’ve tried many times to make it again, but it can never be like theirs,” she says.
Franchir la porte du Manioky Café, c’est: Stepping through the door of Manioky Café means entering somewhere else, well beyond the plates. The colours and textures catch the eye: wood and straw furniture, tropical plants like the bird of paradise, soothing pastel tones… Every detail radiates warmth and invites you to travel. Old trunks and a miniature airplane are like touches of adventure and escape, discreet but present. While a decorator laid the groundwork, it is above all the hands of Cynthia’s family members that brought the space to life: cousins painted, shaped the arches, and built the banquettes and the counter. The result? A place where collective creativity can be felt in every corner, rooted in family ties while open to the world.
Quatre générations de femmes sont au cœu: Four generations of women are at the heart of the Manioky project: Cynthia Élie, her mother, her grandmother and her daughter Maeva, 20, co-owner of the café. As a child, Maeva had even drawn what she imagined the future café would look like, without knowing whether it would ever open. Today, that drawing is framed and sits on the mantel in the middle of the café’s dining room. Cynthia walks over to show it to us. “She heard me talking about it with passion. She was seven or eight. I was so touched. I’m so happy I kept it,” says the restaurateur.
Le dessin de Maeva, posé sur la cheminée: Maeva’s drawing, sitting on the mantel, evokes the dream of a café imagined long before it opened. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
Pour Cynthia, le Manioky Café est un hom: For Cynthia, Manioky Café is a tribute to her mother’s values and cooking. It was her mother who inspired not only the desire to open a food business, but also the café’s name. The name Manioky, a contraction of “manioc” and “turkey,” recalls the manioc bites stuffed with turkey that she used to cook. “She was ahead of her time in the way she cooked,” Cynthia says, highlighting her mother’s creative spirit: she spiced up the traditional tourtière and transformed dishes from elsewhere, like chop suey. “Manioky” sums up the spirit of the place: a café where Haitian traditions are honoured while being adapted to a modern context.

Derrière la fondation de cet établisseme: Behind the founding of this establishment lies the patience of dough left to rise before it’s turned into something nourishing. Before becoming an entrepreneur, Cynthia Élie followed a completely different path, far from the stove. After years in diagnostic radiology, management and insurance, burnout forced her to stop for almost a year. “Unfortunately, it was a bad thing that brought something good,” she confides. That’s when she came across a space for rent in Repentigny called Chez Élie, like a sign. The desire to open a café, which had been simmering in her mind for two decades, intensified. Encouraged, she decided to take the leap. “One or two weeks later, I made up my mind. I told the owner: ‘OK, let’s do it!’ He believed in the project.”
Se lancer dans cette aventure n’a pas ét: Launching into this adventure wasn’t easy. “It was quite a challenge!” Cynthia admits: she moved fast. She invested her savings, used her credit and plunged into a mountain of paperwork and regulations, all while already being immersed in operations. “If it were just about managing the food, it would be fine, but there’s everything that comes with it,” she sums up. Fortunately, her family was there to support her at every step: aunts, uncles and cousins still lend a hand, whether in the kitchen, in service or on social media. “All the generations come to help me. I’m truly blessed,” she says, her voice full of gratitude.
« Quand on a un rêve, il ne faut jamais: “When you have a dream, you should never give up on it. I gave up on it several times. But in the end, today, I see that it was worth it,” she continues. And more than a restaurant, thanks to its story, Manioky becomes a space where entrepreneurship and creativity meet.
Sandwichs végétariens, au poulet kreyol,: Vegetarian, kreyol chicken and jerk chicken sandwiches sit alongside emblematic Haitian dishes. The griot sandwich, named “Gen Bagay,” is a wink that piques the curiosity of non-Creole speakers. The expression literally means “there is something,” and this sandwich is one of the café’s most popular, according to Cynthia.
Mais les plats offerts ne se limitent pa: But the dishes on offer are not limited to the classics. Cynthia wants people to discover and rediscover nearly forgotten dishes, like mayi-moulin. It’s a mix of polenta, ground meat and tomato sauce that is similar to lasagna in its construction. “When I served this dish at a brunch at the café, nobody knew what it was. That means even their parents didn’t show them what it was. These are dishes that are being lost, that are part of our culture, of our heritage,” she says.

Un exemple parmi d’autres qui rend encor: It’s one example among others that makes the culinary transmission Cynthia seeks to perpetuate through Manioky Café all the more precious.
« Lors de soirées spéciales, j’aimerais: “At special evenings, I’d like to bring these recipes back. Haitian cuisine is very rich and varied, but many people only know two or three dishes,” she laments. For her, culinary knowledge is being lost from one generation to the next. “Here, young people don’t cook. Everyone goes to the ‘casse-croûte,’ but there are dishes my mother made that, after her generation and maybe mine, will no longer be made.”
Chaque recette est comme une miette de p: Every recipe is like a breadcrumb left along the path of memory. Among these memories, joumou soup holds a special place. This orange, fragrant dish, a symbol of victory and freedom, is tied to a history more than two centuries old: on January 1st, 1804, Claire Heureuse, the wife of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, prepared it to celebrate the freedom regained after the revolution. Once reserved for the colonists, joumou soup became a dish of resistance and celebration for the entire Haitian people. Even today, every year on January 1st, it is prepared and shared in every Haitian home. “Maybe at the end of this year, we’ll open the café and make it,” Cynthia says with a smile. In the meantime, she has come up with a lighter version that keeps the original’s emblematic flavours while remaining easy to serve every day.
Pour elle, cuisiner haïtien, c’est compr: For her, cooking Haitian means understanding a blend of African, Taíno, French and Arab cultures. Corn comes from the Taínos. Many recipes bear the imprint of Africa, notably through the use of tubers like yam. To illustrate her point, Cynthia mentions tomtom sauce kalalou (okra), a fragrant dish from Jérémie, in southern Haiti, similar to foufou sauce graine, but which can also be made with breadfruit. “Knowing where what we eat comes from, what its roots are, is also a mission of the café,” she concludes.
<strong>Un café qui inspire et rassemble: A café that inspires and brings people together
Au-delà de ses recettes, c’est son parco: Beyond its recipes, it is her journey and her determination that make Manioky Café an inspiring place, and Cynthia’s story feeds the entrepreneurial spirit of many. “There are often women who tell me: ‘Ah, it inspires me to get started. When I hear your story, that you had given up on the idea of opening something, and that now it’s been 20 years, it gives me hope.’”
Le café devient ainsi plus qu’un lieu de: The café thus becomes more than a restaurant: it becomes a space for exchange, a table for sharing. “We also have a part where, in our mission, we want to promote entrepreneurship in the community.”
Il y a quelques semaines, le Manioky Caf: A few weeks ago, Manioky Café hosted its very first Skill Swap. The idea was born around a table, with another entrepreneur from the neighbourhood. Together, they were looking for a way to build bridges between communities and to give women entrepreneurs a space to exchange. The concept? Trade your expertise for, say, 30 minutes, and receive another participant’s in return.

L’initiative a réuni une dizaine de femm: The initiative brought together about ten women from diverse backgrounds. “It made for such wonderful exchanges,” Cynthia says happily. For her, this kind of gathering is part of her business’s mission: to make Manioky Café a “third space,” a third place, strong in its Afro-Caribbean roots but open to everyone, where mutual aid and sharing are at the heart of the experience. While Manioky Café is already a place for gathering and passing things on, Cynthia has no intention of stopping there.

Ce qui lui donne aussi de l’énergie, c’e: What also gives her energy is the customers’ reaction, the feeling that they feel at ease as soon as they walk through the door. The clientele reflects the café: diverse. Afro-Caribbeans and “old-stock” Quebecers alike frequent the place.
Cette notion de partage, si chère à Cynt: This notion of sharing, so dear to Cynthia, comes from the Sunday meals taken with family. It’s a tradition found in the Caribbean that dates back to the colonial era. “In the Antilles, every family has a meal on Sunday. During slavery, it was the only day of rest. The enslaved would make a special meal on that occasion. And the whole family would come,” she explains.
Durant son enfance, ces dimanches étaien: During her childhood, those Sundays were a way to maintain family and community ties. “My mother was very hospitable. At our place, she kept the clan together. There was always food for everyone, even for guests who showed up spontaneously.”
Le Manioky Café propose également un ser: Manioky Café also offers catering and events. Themed evenings for Black History Month transported participants to Haiti, New Orleans, Trinidad or Jamaica through a mix of music, costumes and traditional dishes. After more than a year in business, the café also hosts birthdays as well as graduation events, and wants to develop its corporate side.
Et déjà, Cynthia imagine les prochaines: And Cynthia is already imagining the next steps: turning the daytime café into a wine bar at night. When the sun goes down, the coffee cups are put away to make room for stemmed glasses. A cocktail menu designed by a mixologist then invites guests to travel in a different way, with rum, tropical fruits and notes of the islands. Later, she plans to offer oenology workshops to demystify wine, which is often seen as elitist.
À plus long terme, Cynthia rêve encore p: In the longer term, Cynthia dreams even bigger: she would like to open other locations in Montréal, Ottawa, Toronto and the United States, notably in Florida, home to a large Haitian community. “That would be the dream within five years.” At the end of the day, whether over a sandwich, a cocktail or a bowl of joumou soup, Manioky Café, wherever it is, will always continue to represent the same thing: cooking that unites, that passes things on, that takes you travelling.
